catalog_quote: Enrico 1998:116: "First, the interpretation of pitch in Skidegate Haida is not controversial. Skidegate Haida has a simple level-tone system precisely like Masset Haida. The latter was first discussed in my dissertation (1980, revised and published as Enrico 1991) and that analysis was extended to Skidegate in a brief fieldwork report in 1984. ... Though it is true that pitch in Skidegate has a very low "functional load", considerably lower than in Masset ... A light rhyme, as is observed in Enrico (1980, 1991), contains no more than one voiced segment while a heavy rhyme contains more than one, and light rhymes have unmarked low tone while heavy rhymes have unmarked high tone." | Enrico 1998:115-116 n.2: "The main-stressed syllable in an utterance has its rhyme lengthened in this dialect, accompanied by a dip in pitch; main-stressed syllables must have high pitch (tone) and so their rh…

sources.quote: p.44: 'there are suprasegmental distinctions of stress and pitch, though neither of these, in itself, appears to be systemically phonemic. Stress is perhaps best characterized for Haida as the relative loudness of the syllable nucleus, while pitch ... is either high or low.' pp.60-63: 'Suprasegmental features in SkH are at present very poorly understood. Phonetically there are two degrees of pitch--high and low--and three degrees of stress ... In at least one instance, pitch is the basis of a phonemic distinction between forms ... sources.note: Second Skidegate grammar in the Glottolog list; downloaded now from ANLA and scanned: confirms no statable word-stress rule (stress/pitch partly lexically specified, otherwise by unstated phrase-level rules; utterance-final lowering). Should be added to the record's sources.

sources.citation: Hori, Hirofumi. 1998. Pitch in Skidegate Haida: A reply to Enrico. Gengo Kenkyu 114: 121-126 (J-STAGE open access)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Disputes Enrico's transcriptions and defends three phonetic pitch levels predictable from syllable structure; on stress only: 'the sonorant in the /VR/ rhyme of a stressed syllable is lengthened particularly in lento utterances ... He asserts that the high pitch of such a stressed syllable falls, but according to my observation the pitch is maintained throughout the entire syllable.' No word-stress placement rule.
sources.note: Completes the Enrico-Hori exchange the record quotes; downloaded now; silent on stress placement (pitch levels only).
